title: Answer to written question E-002354/2026 on harmonised standards under the Machinery Regulation, given by Executive Vice-President Séjourné for the European Commission
date_evidence: Answer given by Executive Vice-President Séjourné on behalf of the European Commission 6.8.2026
key_claim: The Commission plans to re-cite the majority of machinery harmonised standards under Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 in the fourth quarter of 2026, with presumption of conformity only insofar as they cover the relevant essential requirements; new cybersecurity and AI standards have not yet been delivered; compliance without harmonised standards remains possible.
frame_summary: The Commission presents the Machinery Regulation changeover as a managed re-citation of existing standards, while conceding that cybersecurity and AI standards are undelivered and that harmonised standards are voluntary.
verbatim_quote: The adoption by the Commission and citation in the Official Journal of the EU is planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.
verbatim_list: Those harmonised standards will again be providing the presumption of conformity insofar as they cover relevant EHSRs.
Such new standards have not yet been delivered by the ESOs.
it is possible to comply with the EHSRs, without harmonised standards being applied.

title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2015 of 4 September 2026 amending and repealing Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1586 as regards harmonised standards for machinery drafted in support of Directive 2006/42/EC
key_claim: The Decision, published 7 September 2026, repeals the Directive-era list of machinery harmonised standards with effect from 20 January 2027, and says compliance with a standard confers presumption of conformity from the date its reference is published in the Official Journal.
frame_summary: Treats the end of the Directive-era standards list as a dated legal fact, tied to the repeal of Directive 2006/42/EC on 20 January 2027.
verbatim_quote: Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1586 is repealed with effect from 20 January 2027.
verbatim_list: Compliance with a harmonised standard confers a presumption of conformity with the corresponding essential requirements set out in Union harmonisation legislation from the date of publication of the reference of such standard in the Official Journal of the European Union.
notes: Page read live in the built-in browser on 2 November 2026; quotes copied from the rendered page text.

title: Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on European standardisation, repealing Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012, COM(2026) 780 final
key_claim: The Commission proposes a new standardisation regulation that would allow presumption of conformity to be granted to interim standardisation deliverables until a harmonised standard becomes available; its evaluation puts the current standards-setting time at six years.
frame_summary: Argues that the standards system is too slow for the legislation it serves and proposes interim deliverables that carry presumption of conformity.
verbatim_quote: introducing the possibility to grant presumption of conformity to standardisation deliverables until a harmonised standard becomes available
verbatim_list: the standards-setting process was made faster (from a baseline of more than nine years to six years currently)
notes: Page read live in the built-in browser on 2 November 2026; quotes copied from the rendered page text.

title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
date_evidence: L series 2026/1744 24.7.2026 REGULATION (EU) 2026/1744 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 8 July 2026
key_claim: The Digital Omnibus on AI moves the Machinery Regulation to the sectoral section of the AI Act's product list and requires the Commission to adopt delegated acts amending Annex III of the Machinery Regulation to carry AI requirements; manufacturers may rely on AI Act standards in the interim.
frame_summary: Folds AI-enabled machinery into the Machinery Regulation's own regime, so AI safety requirements reach machines through delegated acts rather than a parallel conformity route.
verbatim_quote: the Commission should be required to adopt delegated acts amending Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2023/1230
verbatim_list: manufacturers should be free to rely on harmonised standards or common specifications referenced or adopted pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2024/1689

title: 20 January 2027: 893 machinery harmonised standards stop giving presumption of conformity
date_evidence: Published 30 September 2026 · Standards Drift · every figure counted from the archived Commission list
key_claim: A register count of the Commission's machinery list: 1,342 distinct references, of which 905 carry a 20 January 2027 end date (884 rows set by Decision (EU) 2026/2015), and no harmonised standard is yet cited in support of Regulation (EU) 2023/1230.
frame_summary: Argues the end of presumption is a dated, row-by-row fact in the Official Journal, while whether the same standards are cited under the Regulation before 20 January 2027 is something the record cannot yet answer.
verbatim_quote: With them the list holds 1,342 distinct references, and 905 references on 910 rows carry the 20 January 2027 end date: 11 rows set by Decision (EU) 2025/1740, 15 by Decision (EU) 2026/546 and 884 by Decision (EU) 2026/2015
verbatim_list: no harmonised standard is yet cited in support of Regulation (EU) 2023/1230

title: Products | UK Regulatory Outlook October 2026
date_evidence: Products | UK Regulatory Outlook October 2026 Published on 28 October 2026
key_claim: A law firm's outlook reports that the Commission proposed replacing the Standardisation Regulation, estimates a cut in standard development time from six years to four, and notes the proposal allows interim deliverables so products can reach the market before a full standard is finished.
frame_summary: Reads the Commission's standardisation proposal as a speed reform that lets products reach the market on interim deliverables, which businesses relying on harmonised standards should watch.
verbatim_quote: It estimates the changes would cut the average time to develop a new standard from six years to four.
verbatim_list: allows interim deliverables, so products can reach the market before a full standard is finished.

title: Why does Presumption of Conformity Matter?
key_claim: A testing and certification vendor notes that most standards do not address protection against corruption (requirement 1.1.9), that EN 50742 is being developed for it, and that with presumption the burden shifts to market authorities.
frame_summary: Explains why presumption of conformity lowers manufacturer risk and where the gap in cybersecurity coverage sits, from a vendor selling conformity services.
verbatim_quote: Most standards do not currently address Protection against corruption, EHSR 1.1.9.
verbatim_list: the general burden shifts away from the manufacturer and to the market authorities or complainants who need to prove that the product doesn’t comply with the EHSR requirements.
